title: Classical optimization with imaginary time block encoding on quantum computers: The MaxCut problem
abstract_summary: The authors introduce ITE-BE, an exact block-encoding implementation of imaginary-time evolution with analytically determined parameters that requires no variational optimization, and apply it to the MaxCut problem. They show that ITE-BE converges to ground states for small 3-regular graphs, demonstrate that combining ITE-BE with QAOA boosts post-selection success and solution quality (with shallow QAOA plus ITE-BE outperforming deeper QAOA), and discuss scalability limits due to exponentially decaying post-selection probabilities.
methodology_description: The authors evaluate block-encoding-based imaginary time evolution (ITE-BE) for solving the MaxCut problem and investigate a hybrid protocol that prepends a QAOA state-preparation layer to ITE-BE (QAOA+ITE-BE). They map MaxCut to a diagonal problem Hamiltonian HC = -(1/2) sum_{<j,k>} w_{jk}(I - Z_j Z_k). Because Z_j Z_k terms commute, the imaginary-time propagator factorizes exactly into per-edge terms e^{-τ w_{jk} Z_j Z_k / 2}. Each two-qubit non-unitary propagator is implemented via an exact block-encoding circuit (RBM-inspired), using one ancilla qubit per block with post-selection on the ancilla being |0>. For the special case of the transverse initial state |+>^{⊗N} the first layer is implemented with a corrected block that deterministically applies the first propagators and avoids post-selection on those edges forming a maximal matching. The pure ITE-BE protocol starts from |+>^{⊗N} and applies the per-edge block-encoded propagators (with ancilla reuse via mid-circuit measurement/reset), measuring data qubits only after completing all blocks and successful post-selection. The hybrid protocol prepares an input state with a p-level QAOA circuit using near-optimal parameters from prior work (Ref. [49]) and then applies ITE-BE. Numerical experiments use Qiskit AerSimulator to simulate circuits on unweighted 3-regular graphs (u3R) with N=6..12 nodes (100 random instances for non-bipartite u3R and 40 instances for bipartite u3R), vary imaginary time τ in [0,2], use 1e5 measurement shots per graph per τ, and repeat each configuration 10 times. Performance metrics recorded are approximation ratio r, probability of obtaining an optimal solution popt, and the post-selection success rate. Results report 99.7% (≈3σ) uncertainty intervals and compare pure ITE-BE (p=0) vs QAOA+ITE-BE at multiple p levels (p = 4,6,8,10,12).
experimental_setup: All experiments are classical simulations using Qiskit AerSimulator. Graph instances are generated with networkx (unweighted 3-regular graphs). Circuits simulate N data qubits plus a single ancilla qubit reused by mid-circuit measure/reset; circuit depths scale O(|E|) for ITE-BE and O(p|E| + |E|) for QAOA+ITE-BE. Measurements are in the computational basis after successful ancilla post-selection.
experiment_input: Randomly generated unweighted 3-regular graphs (u3R) using networkx. For non-bipartite experiments: 100 random instances per graph size N ∈ {6,8,10,12}; for bipartite experiments: 40 random instances per size N ∈ {6,8,10,12}. Edge weights w_{jk}=1, each node degree 3, number of edges |E| = 3N/2. No additional preprocessing other than generation; special-case maximal matching chosen to deterministically implement first-layer blocks when starting from |+>^{⊗N}.
experiment_process: 1) For pure ITE-BE: prepare |+>^{⊗N}; partition edges into V1 (maximal matching) and V2 (remaining edges). Apply corrected deterministic block-encoding circuits (no post-selection) for edges in V1; apply generic block-encoding circuits with ancilla and post-selection for edges in V2. Reuse a single ancilla qubit via mid-circuit measurement/reset; if any ancilla measurement yields |1> during V2 blocks the shot is discarded. Vary τ from 0 to 2 and run 1e5 shots per τ per graph; repeat each τ 10 times. 2) For QAOA+ITE-BE: prepare a p-level QAOA state |ψ(β,γ)⟩ with near-optimal parameters taken from Ref. [49] (no parameter optimization performed in this work), with p ∈ {4,6,8,10,12}. Use that state as input and apply the same ITE-BE per-edge block-encoding sequence (generic blocks with ancilla and post-selection). For both protocols measure data qubits only after successful post-selection, compute metrics, and aggregate results across instances to report means and 99.7% uncertainty intervals.
experiment_output: Per-τ, per-graph outputs are (i) approximation ratio r = C(z)/C_max (averaged over successful shots), (ii) probability of obtaining an optimal solution popt = N_opt/N_tot (N_tot: number of successful post-selected measurement outcomes), and (iii) post-selection success rate (probability that all required ancilla measurements are |0>). Results are summarized across instances (mean ± 3σ). Baselines: pure ITE-BE (p=0) and QAOA outputs at τ=0 using the same near-optimal parameters; comparisons focus on convergence of r and popt with τ and dependence of post-selection success on τ, N and QAOA level p.

experiment_parameters.circuit_depth_estimate: O(|E|) for ITE-BE; O(p|E| + |E|) for QAOA+ITE-BE
experiment_parameters.block_encoding_parameters: W_jk = (1/2) arccos[exp(-|τ w_jk|)], s_jk = sign(W_jk); alternate parameters for deterministic correction provided in Appendix A
experiment_parameters.post_selection: required for generic blocks (shots discarded if any ancilla measured |1| in V2); deterministic first-layer blocks applied on matching edges when starting from |+>^{⊗N}

hardware_details.classical_resources: Simulations ran on computing resources acknowledged from Center for Advanced Research Computing (CARC) at USC and NERSC (DOE)

reproducibility_notes: No public code repository or data archive is provided in the preprint. The authors report sufficient implementation details to reproduce experiments: graph generation via networkx (unweighted 3-regular graphs), block-encoding parameter formulas (Eq. 8 and Appendix A), use of QAOA parameters from Ref. [49], τ sweep, shots=1e5 and 10 repetitions. Reproduction should be feasible using Qiskit AerSimulator and networkx, but exact random-instance seeds and the QAOA parameter vectors used from Ref. [49] are not included in the paper text; those would need to be obtained from the cited reference or requested from the authors.
key_findings: [supported] The ITE-BE (imaginary-time block encoding) method converges to the MaxCut ground state for the tested unweighted 3-regular graphs (N = 6–12) as imaginary time τ increases (simulations show convergence by about τ ≈ 2).
[supported] The post-selection success rate of the block-encoding implementation decays exponentially with increasing imaginary time τ and with problem size N (observed in simulations).

[supported] Combining QAOA state preparation with ITE-BE (QAOA+ITE-BE) produces faster convergence to the ground state and higher post-selection success than starting from the equal-superposition |+>^N state; for N = 12 and p = 12 the post-selection rate improved by roughly an order of magnitude in the reported simulations.

[supported] Shallow QAOA circuits followed by ITE-BE can outperform deeper QAOA circuits for the studied instances—i.e., a trade-off between QAOA depth p and imaginary time τ exists and shallower QAOA plus ITE-BE can give better practical performance.

[supported] For the special/transverse initial state |+>^N, a modified block-encoding circuit and parameter choice allow a deterministic application (correction for failed post-selection) of the first layer, reducing the need to discard runs.

[supported] Bipartite 3-regular graphs exhibit faster convergence under ITE-BE and a post-selection success rate that plateaus at smaller τ relative to non-bipartite graphs (observed in simulations and spectral analysis).

[supported] The proposed implementations require (with ancilla reuse) about N+1 qubits and have circuit depth O(|E|) per imaginary-time layer (theoretical resource accounting tied to the block-encoding design).

[speculative] The authors suggest ITE-BE-based methods are a promising direction for larger-scale combinatorial optimization, but practical use is limited by exponential decay of post-selection success—addressing this is left as future work.

[speculative] The statement that ITE-BE 'guarantees convergence to the optimal solution' is made in the paper; this is theoretically true under the standard imaginary-time assumptions (nonzero initial overlap and effectively infinite sampling / successful post-selection), but in practice is limited by exponentially small post-selection probability and finite-sampling effects.
results_summary: The paper introduces and evaluates ITE-BE, an exact block-encoding implementation of imaginary-time evolution for solving MaxCut, and a hybrid protocol QAOA+ITE-BE. Simulation experiments (Qiskit Aer) on random unweighted 3-regular graphs with N = 6–12 show that both ITE-BE and QAOA+ITE-BE converge to ground states as imaginary time τ increases (convergence observed near τ ≈ 2). Post-selection success falls off exponentially with τ and problem size, but initializing ITE-BE with a QAOA-prepared state improves both convergence speed and post-selection rates (by about an order of magnitude in one reported case). Special handling for the transverse initial state reduces post-selection overhead for the first layer. Bipartite instances converge faster and show plateaus in success rates. Resource-wise, the approach uses N+1 qubits (with ancilla reuse) and O(|E|) circuit depth per ITE layer. The authors note scalability limits and that demonstrating quantum advantage would require substantially larger devices (≫12 qubits).
performance_claims: Convergence to ground state observed by τ ≈ 2 in simulations for unweighted 3-regular graphs with N = 6–12 [supported].
Post-selection success rate decays exponentially with τ and N (observed in the numerical results) [supported].
Using QAOA-prepared initial states (e.g., p = 12) increased post-selection rate by about an order of magnitude for N = 12 at τ = 2 compared to starting from |+>^N [supported].
Approximation ratio r and probability of obtaining optimal solution popt increase monotonically with τ; r in pure ITE-BE starts from 0.5 at τ = 0 for the tested ensembles [supported].
Simulations used 1e5 shots per τ per graph instance and repeated runs to build statistics (methodological detail reported) [supported].

Resource claim: the protocol can be implemented with N+1 qubits (reusing a single ancilla) and circuit depth O(|E|) per ITE application; full protocol with p-level QAOA has depth O(p|E|+|E|) [supported].

Authors state that demonstrating quantum advantage would require access to more than 100 qubits, given current classical solver capabilities (argumentative estimate, not experimentally demonstrated) [speculative].
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate quantum advantage; results are small-scale classical simulations (N = 6–12). The authors explicitly note classical SDP and exact solvers already handle much larger instances and estimate that demonstrating advantage would require >100 qubits. Thus any claim about quantum advantage is speculative and contingent on overcoming the exponential post-selection cost and having significantly larger quantum hardware.
limitations: The ITE-BE block-encoding approach has a post-selection success rate that decays exponentially with imaginary time τ and problem size N (author-stated).

Practical applicability is limited by the exponential decay in post-selection success — without improvements to post-selection or convergence speed the method is not practical for large problems (author-stated).
Demonstrations are limited to small-scale simulations (unweighted 3-regular graphs with N ≤ 12); quantum advantage would require access to >100 qubits (author-stated).

The block-encoding implementation requires ancilla qubits and post-selection; improving success via amplitude amplification would require additional ancilla and increase circuit depth (author-stated).

The study focuses mainly on the MaxCut problem (and mostly on unweighted 3-regular graphs); applicability and performance on other combinatorial problems, weighted graphs, or non-commuting Hamiltonians is not demonstrated (author-stated/in-scope).
There is a trade-off between QAOA circuit depth p and required imaginary time τ: shallower QAOA + larger τ or deeper QAOA + smaller τ (author-stated).
[inferred] All results are from ideal (noise-free) circuit simulations (Qiskit AerSimulator); no analysis of hardware noise, gate errors, or decoherence is provided.
[inferred] Ancilla reuse relies on mid-circuit measurements and resets; that capability may not be available or may be costly on many current quantum hardware platforms.
[inferred] Circuit depth scales as O(|E|) (and O(p|E|) when combined with QAOA); for dense or large graphs this depth may be prohibitive on near-term devices.
[inferred] The deterministic correction for failed post-selection is presented for special initial states (e.g., transverse |+>); generalization to arbitrary initial states is not shown.

[inferred] The QAOA parameters used were taken from prior literature (tuned for approximation ratio r) rather than optimized here; thus the combined-method performance may not reflect jointly optimized parameters.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — ITE-BE is an exact block-encoding implementation of imaginary-time evolution with analytically determined parameters that requires no variational optimization and converges to ground states for small 3-regular graphs.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Prepending a shallow QAOA state-preparation layer to ITE-BE (QAOA+ITE-BE) boosts post-selection success and solution quality, with shallow QAOA+ITE-BE outperforming deeper QAOA alone on tested instances.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The protocol is evaluated on small instances (N=6..12) using ancilla reuse and deterministic first-layer blocks to reduce post-selection overhead, suggesting potential NISQ-era applicability for small problem sizes.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical metrics (approximation ratio r, optimal-solution probability popt, and post-selection success rate) show improved convergence with ITE time τ and improved performance for QAOA+ITE-BE relative to baselines on the simulated instances.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The work reuses a single ancilla with mid-circuit measurement/reset and leverages deterministic correction on a maximal matching to avoid some post-selection, reducing qubit requirements.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — QAOA parameters are taken from prior literature (no optimization in this work), indicating the hybrid protocol can leverage precomputed variational parameters rather than in-situ optimization.
